13630:
To repeal something means to officially and completely cancel a law, rule, or regulation that was previously established, so that it no longer exists or has any legal effect. Think of it as "officially undoing" a law — wiping it off the books entirely.

A key thing to understand right away: repeal is a formal, authoritative act. It is not someone simply deciding to ignore a law, or a court saying a law was unfair. It is the official removal of a law by a body that has the power to do so — usually a parliament, congress, or legislature.
The Key Idea: Gone, Not Just Changed

The most important thing about "repeal" is that it means complete removal, not just modification.

When a law is repealed, it does not get weakened, adjusted, or suspended. It is gone. It ceases to exist as a law. Nobody is bound by it anymore. This is what separates "repeal" from words like "amend" (which means to change a law, while keeping it alive).

Think of it this way: if a law were a rule written on a blackboard, amending it would be erasing some words and rewriting them. Repealing it would be erasing the whole thing entirely.
Who Repeals, and What Gets Repealed?

Who repeals: Typically, the same body that created the law — a government, a parliament, a congress, or a legislature. A new government might repeal laws passed by a previous government. A legislature can repeal its own old laws.

What gets repealed: Almost always a law, act, statute, regulation, or policy — things that were formally enacted in the first place. You repeal things that were officially created through a legal or governmental process.

Common things that get repealed:

  • National laws and acts (e.g., "Congress repealed the act.")
  • Tax laws (e.g., "The government repealed the fuel tax.")
  • Bans and prohibitions (e.g., "They repealed the ban on imports.")
  • Constitutional amendments, in some cases

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important as knowing what it does.

Repeal does not mean "ignore." If a government simply stops enforcing a law but doesn't formally remove it, that is not a repeal. The law still technically exists on paper.

Repeal does not apply to personal decisions. You wouldn't say "I repealed my decision to go to the gym." It is a legal/governmental term, not an everyday personal one.

Repeal does not mean "suspend." Suspending a law means putting it on pause temporarily. Repealing it means ending it permanently.

Repeal is not the same as a court striking down a law. When a court (like a Supreme Court) declares a law unconstitutional and invalid, that is usually described as "striking down" or "overturning" the law — not repealing it. Repeal specifically refers to a legislative (law-making) body removing a law, not a judicial (court) body.

These words are often confused with "repeal," but they have distinct meanings:

Amend: To change or modify a law. The law still lives, but parts of it are altered. ("They amended the contract to include a new clause.") Repeal removes the whole thing; amendment edits it.

Revoke: To cancel a specific permission, license, or privilege granted to a person or entity. ("Her driving license was revoked.") Revoke is more personal and specific; repeal is broader and legislative.

Abolish: To formally bring something to an end — often used for institutions, systems, or practices, not just laws. ("They abolished slavery.") Abolish has a wider, more sweeping feel. Repeal is specifically about cancelling a formal law or act.

Annul: To declare something void — as if it never existed or was never valid. Often used in contexts like marriage ("The marriage was annulled."). Repeal doesn't pretend the law never existed; it simply ends it going forward.

Rescind: To cancel an order, decision, or agreement, often in a business or contractual context. ("The company rescinded the job offer.") Rescind is less formal and legislative than repeal.

The cleanest summary: repeal is specifically and almost exclusively used for the legislative cancellation of a law or formal act.

Here are examples showing how "repeal" is used naturally:

  • "Parliament voted to repeal the outdated law."
  • "Activists spent years campaigning to repeal the ban."
  • "The new president promised to repeal several regulations introduced by his predecessor."
  • "The prohibition on alcohol was repealed in 1933, ending the era of Prohibition in the United States."
  • "Critics argued that repealing the environmental law would cause serious harm."
  • "Once the law was repealed, businesses were free to operate without those restrictions."

Notice that you can use repeal in different tenses: repeal, repeals, repealed, repealing.
A Real-World Example to Make It Stick

One of the most famous real-world examples of repeal is the 18th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which introduced Prohibition — making it illegal to produce or sell alcohol. It was later repealed by the 21st Amendment in 1933, which cancelled the ban entirely and made alcohol legal again.

This example shows the essence of the word perfectly: a law that existed was formally, officially, and completely removed by the appropriate authority, so it no longer had any force.

If you had to carry just one definition in your head:

To repeal means to officially and permanently cancel a law or formal rule, so that it no longer has any legal effect.
13631: Repel means to push something away, or to force something to stay away. Think of it as the exact opposite of attract. Where attract pulls things closer, repel drives them apart or keeps them at a distance. This pushing away can happen in three distinct ways — physically, emotionally, and practically/materially.
Sense 1 — To push back or drive away by force

This is the most literal meaning. When a force pushes something away, or when a person or group actively drives something back, we say they repel it.

The clearest example in nature is magnets. Hold two magnets with the same poles facing each other, and they push each other away — they repel each other. No matter how hard you try, an invisible force keeps them apart.

In a military context, if an army successfully fights off an enemy attack and forces the attackers to retreat, they have repelled the attack. The key idea is that something was coming and it was driven back.

"The soldiers repelled the enemy's advance."
"The two poles of the magnets repelled each other."
Sense 2 — To cause strong disgust or aversion in someone

This is the most common everyday use, and it's important to understand how strong this feeling is. To be repelled by something is not just to dislike it quietly — it is to feel such strong disgust that you experience an almost physical urge to turn away, move away, or get as far from it as possible. It is a powerful, instinctive reaction.

A smell, a sight, a behavior, or a person's attitude can all repel someone. The subject doing the repelling is the thing causing the disgust, and the object is the person being affected.

"The sight of the infected wound repelled him completely."
"Her cruelty repelled everyone who met her."
"I was repelled by the way he treated the staff."

Notice that last example: you can say either "It repelled me" or "I was repelled by it" — both are grammatically correct and mean the same thing.

An important nuance here: being repelled is involuntary. You don't decide to feel repelled; the feeling comes to you as a natural reaction, almost like a reflex. This is what separates repel from simply dislike. You might dislike a bland meal and quietly push the plate away. But a plate of maggots would repel you — you'd feel a gut-level, urgent need to look away or leave. The word carries that intensity.
Sense 3 — To resist or block something from passing through

Some materials or substances are designed to prevent something from entering, penetrating, or coming near. When they successfully do this, we say they repel that thing.

"This jacket repels water." (Water cannot soak in; it runs right off the surface.)
"The spray repels mosquitoes." (Mosquitoes are driven away and kept from coming near.)
"The coating on the pan repels grease."

This is the exact reason we call insect-repelling products repellents — they repel (keep away) insects. The word "repellent" comes directly from this use.

Repel is always a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object. It must repel something or someone. You cannot use it without specifying what is being pushed away.

✅ "The smell repelled the guests."
❌ "The smell repelled." ← This is incomplete. Repelled whom? Repelled what?

The antonym of repel is attract — to pull something toward you, or to make someone feel drawn in. These two words are perfect mirrors of each other:

  • A magnet can either attract iron filings or repel them.
  • A person's warmth might attract others; their arrogance might repel them.
  • A bright light attracts moths, but certain chemicals repel them.

Understanding this pair helps anchor the meaning of repel firmly in your mind.

Repellent (adjective) — describes something that repels in the emotional sense. "A repellent personality" means a personality so off-putting that people instinctively want to stay away.

Repellent (noun) — a substance designed to keep something away. "Insect repellent," "mosquito repellent," "tick repellent."

Repulsive (adjective) — very similar to repellent in the emotional sense, but often even stronger. If something is repulsive, it causes a deep, almost nauseating disgust. "The scene was repulsive." You can think of repellent and repulsive as near-synonyms in everyday use, with repulsive being the more intense of the two.

Repulsion (noun) — the feeling or force of being repelled. "She felt a wave of repulsion when she heard his words." In physics, it also refers to the force by which like charges or magnetic poles push each other apart.

The single thread connecting all three senses of repel is this: something is being pushed away, or kept away. Whether it's an army being driven back, a person being disgusted into moving away, or water being blocked from soaking through a surface — the core idea is always the same. Repel is a word about distance, separation, and resistance. Wherever you see it, ask yourself: what is being pushed away, and by what? The answer will always make the meaning clear.
13632:
When something is repellent, it makes you want to pull back, turn away, or stay far from it. It produces a strong feeling of disgust, discomfort, or aversion — a gut-level reaction that says "I don't want to be near this."

Think of a magnet. When you hold two magnets with the same poles facing each other, they push each other away. That pushing-away force is exactly the feeling "repellent" captures — except here, it's a feeling inside a person reacting to something outside them.

The adjective can describe three broad categories:

1. Something your senses experience

A smell, a sight, a taste, or a texture can be repellent. This is a physical, almost instinctive disgust — your body wants to move away.

  • The rotten food had a repellent odour.
  • The wound looked repellent; she had to look away.

2. Someone's personality, attitude, or behaviour

A person can be repellent if they behave in a way that makes others deeply uncomfortable or disgusted. This isn't just mild rudeness — it's something that makes people actively want to avoid that person.

  • His cruelty and selfishness made him repellent to everyone around him.
  • She found his smug, dismissive attitude completely repellent.

3. An idea, belief, or action

Abstract things — a political belief, a moral stance, an act of violence, a harmful ideology — can also be repellent. Here, the aversion is moral or intellectual rather than sensory.

  • The idea of torturing animals is repellent to most people.
  • He found the regime's propaganda repellent and refused to repeat it.

"Repellent" is a strong word. It sits well above "unpleasant" or "off-putting" on the scale of disgust. Here's a rough sense of the ladder:

Dislikeable → Unpleasant → Off-putting → Repellent → Revolting → Nauseating

It signals that the reaction is not just mild annoyance. Something repellent produces a deep, visceral, almost involuntary urge to distance yourself from it. However, it is slightly more controlled and measured in tone than "revolting" or "nauseating," which suggest a more extreme physical reaction (like feeling sick).
An Important Nuance: Objective vs. Subjective

Sometimes "repellent" describes something that is objectively, universally disgusting (most people would agree a rotting corpse smells repellent).

Other times, it is personal. What one person finds repellent, another may not. For example:

  • She found abstract art repellent — she simply couldn't connect with it.
  • He found the culture of excessive wealth repellent, though many admired it.

In these personal cases, "repellent" tells you as much about the speaker's values and sensibilities as it does about the thing being described.
The Flip Side — What "Repellent" Is Not

To understand a word fully, it helps to see its opposite. The antonym of repellent is attractive or appealing — things that draw you toward them. Some related antonyms: inviting, charming, alluring, pleasant.

If something attractive pulls you in like a magnet, something repellent pushes you out just as powerfully.

"Repellent" describes anything — a smell, a person, a behaviour, or an idea — that provokes a strong feeling of disgust or aversion and makes you want to distance yourself from it. It's stronger than merely "unpleasant," but not as extreme as "revolting." It can describe both physical experiences and moral or emotional reactions, and it can be either universal (most people would agree) or deeply personal (a matter of individual taste or values).

When you use this word, you are signalling that the reaction is powerful, real, and hard to ignore — not a casual dislike, but something that genuinely repels.
13633:
To repent means to feel deep, genuine sorrow for something wrong that you have done — and to sincerely wish you had not done it — while also having a strong desire to change your ways and not repeat that wrong.

Notice that definition has three parts. All three matter:

  1. You feel deep sorrow (not just mild embarrassment)
  2. You recognize what you did was genuinely wrong
  3. You have a desire to change — to do better going forward

This is important because repentance is never just a feeling you sit with. It always points forward. A person who repents is not just crying about the past; they are making an inner commitment to be different.
The One Thing That Makes "Repent" Unique

Many words describe feeling bad about something. What makes repent stand out is the combination of moral guilt + inner transformation.

Think of it this way:

  • You can regret eating too much cake. → That's just disappointment in an outcome.
  • You can regret a car accident you didn't cause. → That's sadness, not guilt.
  • But you repent when you did something morally wrong, you know it was wrong, and you genuinely want to become the kind of person who would not do it again.

Repentance is always personal, always moral, and always involves a turning of the heart.

In a religious context

This is where the word is most at home, and where its full weight is felt. In religions like Christianity, Islam, and Judaism, to repent means to turn away from sin — to stand before God (or your conscience) and say: "I did wrong. I am sorry. I will not go back to that." It is considered a serious, sacred act, not a casual one.

"The preacher called on his congregation to repent and seek forgiveness."

In everyday, secular use

Outside of religion, the word is used more broadly but carries the same emotional seriousness. It means to deeply regret a wrong decision or harmful action — one that hurt others or violated your own values.

"Years later, he repented the way he had treated his old friend."
"She repented her dishonesty the moment she saw the hurt on his face."

In secular use, "repent" is slightly formal or literary in tone. In casual conversation, people more often say "I deeply regret" or "I'm so sorry for what I did." But when a writer or speaker uses repent in a non-religious context, they are deliberately signaling a deeper, more profound kind of remorse — one that touches the person's character, not just their actions.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The verb repent can be used in several patterns:

1. Repent + of + something
This is the most traditional and common pattern.

"He repented of his greed."
"She repented of every cruel word she had ever spoken."

2. Repent + for + something
Very similar in meaning, and widely accepted.

"He repented for his past mistakes."

3. Repent + something (direct object, no preposition)
Used more in literary or religious writing.

"He repented his betrayal."

4. Repent alone (no object)
The speaker doesn't name a specific wrong — just the act of repenting itself.

"It is never too late to repent."
"He lived a selfish life and refused to repent."

Repent vs. Regret
Regret is wider and softer. You can regret things that were not your fault, were not morally wrong, or were simply unfortunate choices. Repent is narrower and deeper — it is always about something morally wrong that you did.

You regret a missed opportunity. You repent a betrayal.

Repent vs. Apologize
Apologizing is an outward act — something you say to another person. Repenting is an inward act — a change of heart within yourself. Ideally you do both, but they are not the same thing. Someone can apologize without truly repenting (just going through the motions), and someone can repent sincerely in their heart without ever getting the chance to apologize.

Repent vs. Feel remorse
Remorse is the painful feeling of guilt about what you've done. It looks backward. Repentance includes that feeling but goes further — it also looks forward with a commitment to change. Remorse without repentance is just suffering in guilt. Repentance turns that guilt into action and transformation.

Repent vs. Confess
Confessing means admitting what you did — out loud, to another person or to God. Repenting is the deeper emotional and moral shift that happens within you. Confession is often part of repentance, but repentance is bigger than confession.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

It is worth understanding that repent is not a light word. It carries moral seriousness and, even in non-religious use, a slight spiritual gravity. When someone says they repent something, they are not saying "oops." They are saying: "I know I did something wrong. I feel the weight of it. And I am choosing to be different."

This is what makes it a powerful and precise word — it captures not just an emotion, but an entire moral experience.
13634:
Repentance is the act of genuinely feeling sorry for something wrong you have done — and, crucially, deciding to change because of it.

Notice that definition has two parts: the feeling and the turning away. Both are essential. If you only feel bad but don't intend to change, that's not repentance. If you change your behavior but feel nothing about what you did wrong, that's not repentance either. True repentance is both happening together.
Breaking it down piece by piece

Repentance has four inner layers, each building on the one before it:

1. Recognition
You first have to honestly see that what you did was wrong. Not making excuses, not blaming others, not telling yourself it wasn't a big deal. You look at your action clearly and admit: "That was wrong. I did that."

2. Remorse
This is the genuine pain, sorrow, or regret you feel about the wrong you committed. It's not just surface-level embarrassment or the discomfort of getting caught. It's a real, inner ache — a sincere sense of "I shouldn't have done that, and I wish I hadn't."

3. Resolution
Here, you make a firm inner decision: "I will not do this again." You turn away from the wrong action — not because you're forced to, but because you genuinely don't want to be the kind of person who does such things. This is the "turning point" in repentance. Many people describe it as a change of direction from the inside.

4. Making amends (when possible)
Repentance often leads naturally to trying to fix the harm you caused — apologizing to someone you hurt, returning something you took, correcting a lie you told. This isn't always possible (some damage can't be fully undone), but the desire to repair things is usually part of genuine repentance.
How repentance differs from words that look similar

These words are neighbors of repentance, but they're not the same thing:

Repentance vs. Regret
Regret is broader and more passive. You can regret eating too much cake, regret missing a flight, or regret a haircut — things that weren't even morally wrong. Repentance, on the other hand, is specifically about moral wrongdoing, and it carries a commitment to change. Regret says, "I wish that hadn't happened." Repentance says, "I was wrong, and I am going to be different."

Repentance vs. Remorse
Remorse is the painful, guilty feeling you experience after doing something wrong. It's one ingredient of repentance — the emotional part — but repentance is bigger. You can feel remorse and still go back to doing the same wrong thing. Repentance takes that remorse and does something with it: it leads to change.

Repentance vs. Guilt
Guilt is also just a feeling — the internal signal that tells you something you did violated your own sense of right and wrong. Guilt can be healthy (it pushes you toward repentance) or it can become unhealthy (when it paralyzes you, keeps you stuck, and leads nowhere). Repentance is what happens when you respond to guilt productively: you face what you did, feel genuine sorrow, and change.

Repentance vs. Apology
An apology is something you say to another person. Repentance is something that happens inside you. You can give an apology without repentance (hollow, insincere words). And you can have deep repentance even without having the chance to apologize yet (perhaps the person is no longer in your life). Apology is an outward act; repentance is an inward transformation.
Where and how this word is used

In religion and spirituality
This is where "repentance" is used most often, and where it carries the deepest weight. In Christianity, Islam, Judaism, and many other traditions, repentance is a central spiritual act — turning away from wrongdoing and returning to God or to one's moral path. It's seen not as a sign of weakness but as one of the most courageous and important things a person can do. Religious teachings often describe repentance as the beginning of healing and renewal.

"The preacher called on his congregation to live lives of sincere repentance."

In everyday moral life
Outside of religious settings, repentance describes the same inner process when someone truly comes to terms with harm they've caused — to another person, to a community, or even to themselves — and commits to doing better.

"After years of hurting people with his anger, there was a quiet but unmistakable repentance in the way he now spoke and acted."

In formal or public contexts
You'll sometimes see it used to describe someone's public acknowledgment of wrongdoing, like a criminal expressing repentance before a court, or a public figure owning up to serious mistakes.

"The judge noted the defendant's evident repentance and took it into account in sentencing."

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important as knowing what it does.

  • Repentance is not just saying "sorry." Words without inner change are hollow. Real repentance is proven over time through behavior, not just declared in a moment.
  • Repentance is not self-punishment. Some people confuse repentance with torturing themselves with guilt endlessly. Genuine repentance acknowledges wrong, feels appropriate sorrow, and then moves forward — it doesn't keep you trapped in self-loathing.
  • Repentance is not weakness. It actually demands tremendous honesty and courage. Admitting you were wrong, facing the harm you caused, and committing to change is one of the harder things a person can do. It's far easier to make excuses or deny wrongdoing.
  • Repentance is not always a single moment. Sometimes it's a gradual process. A person might begin to see that they were wrong, slowly feel the weight of it, and over days or weeks arrive at a genuine change of heart. The word can describe that entire journey.
A simple mental image to hold onto

Think of repentance like realizing you've been walking in the wrong direction.

First, you notice you're going the wrong way (recognition). Then you feel the frustration and regret of the wrong path you've been on (remorse). Then you stop, turn around, and start walking the right way (resolution). And if you've knocked something over while going the wrong direction, you go back and pick it up (making amends).

The key image is the turning around — which is, at heart, what repentance is all about.
Repentance is the genuine, heartfelt acknowledgment that you have done something wrong, accompanied by real sorrow for it and a sincere commitment to change your ways.
13635:
When someone is repentant, they feel deep, sincere sorrow for something wrong they have done — and, crucially, they also have a genuine desire to make things right or to not repeat that wrong.

It is not a surface-level feeling. It goes to the core of a person's conscience.
Breaking It Down: Two Things Happening at Once

Being repentant always involves two things together, not just one:

  1. Deep remorse — a genuine feeling of guilt and sorrow about the wrong committed. Not just embarrassment that you got caught, but real inner distress about the fact that you did something wrong.
  2. A sincere desire to change or make amends — the person doesn't just feel bad and move on. They want to correct the wrong, repair the damage, or at the very least, never do it again.

If only the first part is present — you feel bad but have no desire to change — that is not truly being repentant. And if only the second part is present — you want to change but feel no genuine sorrow — that is not repentant either. Both must be present together.

People say "I'm sorry" for all kinds of things — bumping into someone on the street, being late to a meeting, forgetting someone's birthday. These uses of "sorry" are polite expressions, often not deeply felt.

Repentant is much heavier. It implies:

  • A genuine moral wrong has been committed (not just an accident or minor inconvenience)
  • The person has reflected on what they did
  • They are genuinely troubled by it inside
  • They sincerely want to do better

A person can apologize without being repentant. But a repentant person always feels something deeply and sincerely. The word carries real emotional and moral weight.
An Important Nuance: Inward Feeling vs. Outward Appearance

Repentant can describe:

  • A true inner state — what the person actually feels inside. "He was truly repentant; he couldn't sleep at night thinking about the harm he had caused."
  • The outward expression of that feeling — how they appear, what they show to others. "She walked in with a repentant look and immediately asked for forgiveness."

This is worth knowing because sometimes people appear repentant without truly feeling it. The word can be used for both, so context matters. When someone says another person "looked repentant," it doesn't necessarily confirm that the feeling is genuine — only that they showed the signs of it.

Repentant is used for morally significant wrongs — things involving betrayal, harm, dishonesty, cruelty, or serious mistakes that hurt others or violate one's own values.

You would not say "I am repentant about burning my toast." That would sound strange because the word carries moral weight.

You would say it for things like:

  • Lying to someone you love
  • Betraying a trust
  • Doing something that hurt another person
  • Acting against your own values in a serious way
  • Committing a crime or a grave moral error

It is commonly used in moral, ethical, and religious contexts — where the idea of wrongdoing, guilt, and the desire to change carry deep significance.

Knowing the opposite sharpens the meaning. An unrepentant person:

  • Feels no genuine sorrow for what they did wrong
  • Has no desire to change or make amends
  • May even be proud of what they did, or simply indifferent

"The criminal remained unrepentant to the end, showing no remorse for the lives he had destroyed."

This contrast makes it clear: being repentant is about owning your wrong, deeply, and genuinely wanting better — for yourself and for those you may have harmed.

• "The repentant son came home after years of bad choices and begged his parents for forgiveness."
  • "She was genuinely repentant and volunteered to fix every mistake she had made."
  • "His repentant tone moved the judge, who decided to give him a lighter sentence."
  • "He said he was sorry, but his eyes told a different story — he didn't look the least bit repentant."
  • "A repentant person doesn't just say 'I'm sorry' — they try to make things right."

These words share much of the same meaning and can help you feel the word from different angles:

  • Remorseful — filled with deep regret and guilt for a wrong done
  • Contrite — sincerely sorry and humble about a wrong; often implies a readiness to accept punishment or make amends
  • Penitent — very similar to repentant; often used in religious settings to describe someone who is sorry for their sins and wishes to be forgiven
  • Sorry (in its deepest sense) — when used genuinely and in a serious context, it overlaps with repentant, but it is a milder, more everyday word

Among all of these, repentant and contrite are perhaps the closest to each other. Both carry the sense of genuine moral remorse and the desire to do better.
In a Sentence: How the Word Behaves Grammatically

As an adjective, repentant comes before a noun or after a linking verb:

  • Before a noun: "a repentant sinner," "a repentant look," "a repentant tone"
  • After a linking verb: "He was repentant." "She seemed repentant." "They appeared repentant."

To know someone is repentant is to know three things about them at once:

  1. They did something genuinely wrong.
  2. They feel sincere, deep sorrow about it — not just because of consequences to themselves, but because of the wrong itself.
  3. They want to change, make amends, or at the very least, never do it again.

It is a word that sits at the intersection of conscience, guilt, and the desire to become better. When used honestly, it describes one of the most important moments in a person's moral life — the moment they truly face what they did wrong and decide they cannot simply go on as if nothing happened.
13636:
A repercussion is an indirect, usually unwanted effect that is caused by an action or event — one that spreads outward, often affecting people or things that had nothing to do with the original action.

Think of it this way: you drop a large stone into a still pond. The stone hits the water — that's the action. But then ripples spread outward in every direction, disturbing the water far from where the stone landed. Those ripples are the repercussions. The key point is that the ripples go beyond the original splash.

This word carries several important qualities that you must understand to use it correctly:

1. It is indirect.
A repercussion is not the first thing that happens as a result of an action. It is something that happens further down the chain. If you punch a wall and break your hand, the broken hand is a direct consequence. But if, because of that broken hand, you lose your job, miss your rent, and end up moving out — those are repercussions. They flow from the original action, but indirectly.

2. It tends to be negative.
Repercussions are almost always bad, or at least undesirable. You will almost never hear someone say "the repercussions were wonderful." The word carries a built-in sense of trouble, damage, or difficulty that follows from something.

3. It spreads outward — sometimes to people who were not even involved.
This is what truly sets repercussions apart. A factory in one country shuts down — the workers lose jobs (direct effect). But then local shops lose customers, families struggle to pay school fees, and the town slowly empties out. The shopkeepers and schoolchildren had nothing to do with the factory's decisions, yet they feel the repercussions. The effect radiates outward like those pond ripples.

4. It often appears in the plural.
In everyday use, you will almost always see "repercussions" (plural), not "a repercussion" (singular). This reflects the reality that when something goes wrong, it rarely causes just one ripple — it causes many.

• "The government's decision to raise taxes had serious repercussions for small businesses across the country."

Here, the tax decision is the stone in the pond. Small businesses suffering is one of the ripples — an indirect, negative effect felt by those operating within that economy.

  • "She didn't realize that her careless words would have repercussions for her entire team."

She said something thoughtless. She may have faced personal embarrassment (direct effect), but her team also suffered damage to their reputation — that's a repercussion.

  • "The war in that region had repercussions far beyond its borders."

This is a classic use of the word. The fighting happened in one place, but neighboring countries, global trade, and refugee populations were all shaken by the reverberating effects.
How It Differs from Similar Words

The word most easily confused with repercussion is "consequence."

A consequence is simply any result of an action — it can be direct or indirect, positive or negative, and it is a neutral word. If you study hard and pass your exam, that is a consequence of your studying.

A repercussion, however, is almost always negative, almost always indirect, and carries the specific sense of an effect that ripples outward beyond the immediate situation.

So: every repercussion is a consequence, but not every consequence is a repercussion.

Other related words — like "fallout," "aftermath," and "impact" — are close in meaning, but "repercussion" is unique because of its emphasis on that ripple-like, spreading quality. Fallout and aftermath suggest what is left behind after something happens. Repercussion emphasizes what reverberates outward because something happened.

The word almost always appears with the preposition "of":
"the repercussions of this decision"

Common verbs paired with it: face, feel, suffer, have, cause:

  • "You will have to face the repercussions of your actions."
  • "The entire economy felt the repercussions."
  • "This could cause serious repercussions."

A repercussion is an indirect, negative effect of an action or event that spreads outward — often affecting people, places, or situations far beyond the original point of impact.

Keep that pond-and-ripples image in your mind whenever you see or use this word, and you will never confuse it with anything else.
13637:
Repertoire (noun) refers to the complete set of things a person, group, or system has fully learned, prepared, and is ready to use or perform at any time.

The single most important word hiding inside the meaning of "repertoire" is readiness. A repertoire isn't a wish list of things you'd like to do someday. It isn't things you've vaguely heard of. It is what you have already mastered and can pull out and use right now, on demand.

Think of it like a toolbox. Every tool inside it is one you own, know how to use, and can reach for immediately. That toolbox is your repertoire.
The Three Main Ways It's Used

1. In the performing arts — This is where the word feels most at home. A singer's repertoire is every song she has practiced and can perform on stage tonight. An orchestra's repertoire is every piece of music it has rehearsed and can play in concert. A ballet company's repertoire is every dance production it is currently prepared to stage. The emphasis, again, is on preparedness — these are not pieces they might learn one day. These are pieces they can perform right now.

2. Skills and professional abilities — The word stretches naturally into professional life. A chef's repertoire is every dish he knows how to cook. A doctor's repertoire of treatments is every medical technique she is trained and equipped to use. A programmer's repertoire includes every coding language and problem-solving method he has genuinely mastered. In this sense, your repertoire is essentially your professional toolkit — everything you've built up over time and can draw on when a situation demands it.

3. Habitual behaviors and tactics — People also use "repertoire" more loosely, to describe the range of go-to behaviors or responses someone tends to use. For example: "Sulking, crying, and giving the silent treatment were all part of his repertoire." This usage is often slightly humorous or sarcastic, but the meaning is the same: these are his reliable, practiced moves that he reaches for repeatedly.
The Nuances That Make This Word Precise

Understanding a word deeply means understanding what makes it this word and not some other word. Here's what sets "repertoire" apart:

It always implies readiness, not just knowledge. If a pianist has listened to a Beethoven sonata a thousand times but has never actually practiced playing it, that sonata is not in her repertoire. She knows it exists. She loves it. But it isn't hers to perform yet. Repertoire is about what you can do, not just what you know about.

It implies a range, not a single item. You would never say someone's repertoire is one single joke or one single trick. The word inherently suggests a collection — multiple items, multiple options, multiple capabilities. If you only know one recipe, that's not really a repertoire. When someone has ten recipes they cook brilliantly, that's a cooking repertoire.

It always belongs to someone or something specific. Repertoire is always someone's repertoire. It's personal. You'll always see it paired with ownership: her repertoire, the band's repertoire, the robot's repertoire of responses. It can never just float on its own without a person, group, or entity attached.

It can grow or shrink. A repertoire is not permanently fixed. Performers spend their careers expanding their repertoire by learning new material. Professionals build their repertoire of skills through experience and training. Conversely, if a theatre company stops rehearsing certain plays, those plays eventually leave the active repertoire.

It is not just a general "list" or "collection." A museum has a collection of paintings, but you wouldn't say the paintings are in the museum's "repertoire" — because the museum doesn't perform or do anything with them in that active sense. Repertoire is specifically about what something or someone is actively capable of doing or performing, not simply what they possess or are aware of.

It is also not the same as "potential." Potential is what you could become. Repertoire is what you already are — the skills and works that are fully yours, ready to deploy.

Expand/broaden one's repertoire — to add new skills or works to what you already know. "She took flamenco classes to expand her dance repertoire."

A wide/broad repertoire — having many different things in your collection. "The comedian had a wide repertoire that kept audiences laughing for two hours."

A limited repertoire — having only a narrow set of options. "The new chef had a limited repertoire and could only cook five dishes confidently."

Within someone's repertoire — something a person is capable of doing. "Fixing engines is well within his repertoire."

Outside someone's repertoire — something a person hasn't learned or isn't capable of yet. "Advanced surgery is outside a general practitioner's repertoire."

Add to one's repertoire — the same as expanding it; to learn something new and make it yours. "She added watercolor painting to her repertoire of artistic skills."
A Final Way to Lock It In

If you want one clean sentence to carry with you forever: a repertoire is the full collection of things a person or group has truly mastered and stands ready to perform or use at any moment. It lives at the intersection of ownership, mastery, and readiness — and that combination is what makes this word uniquely useful.
13638:
"Repetitious" is an adjective that describes something involving too much repetition — so much that it becomes boring, tiresome, or pointless. It doesn't just mean something repeats. It means something repeats more than it needs to, and that extra repetition adds nothing of value.

Think of it this way: if a friend tells you the same story twice in a day, fine. But if they tell you the same story five times in a single conversation, never adding anything new, their storytelling is repetitious. The repetition has crossed a line — from useful into unnecessary.

This is important: "repetitious" is almost always a criticism. It is rarely, if ever, a compliment or a neutral observation. When you call something repetitious, you are making a judgment — you are saying this thing repeats itself more than is acceptable, and the excess is a flaw. The word carries a strong sense of tedium and frustration.

This sets it apart from the simple concept of repetition, which can actually be a good thing. A teacher who repeats a key idea twice helps students absorb it. A catchy chorus in a song is enjoyable precisely because it repeats. But the moment that repetition becomes unnecessary and starts to bore or irritate, the word "repetitious" is the right label.

Almost anything that involves communication, behaviour, or creative output can be described as repetitious.

A speech or lecture is repetitious when the speaker keeps circling back to the same point using different words but never actually moving the idea forward. Writing is repetitious when an essay restates its central argument in paragraph after paragraph without developing it or saying anything fresh. Music can be repetitious when it loops the same melody without any progression or variation. A job or daily routine can feel repetitious when it involves doing the exact same actions over and over with no change or challenge. Even a person's conversational habits can be described as repetitious if they constantly bring up the same topics or phrases.
The Key Difference From Similar Words

Three words are often confused with "repetitious," so it's worth understanding exactly how they differ.

Repetitious vs. Repetitive. These two are the most commonly confused, and in casual everyday speech, people use them interchangeably. However, a meaningful difference exists. "Repetitive" is more neutral — it simply describes something that repeats, without necessarily judging it. For example, medical professionals speak of "repetitive strain injuries" caused by performing the same physical motion repeatedly — this is a factual, clinical use with no negative judgment. "Repetitious," by contrast, almost always implies that the repetition is excessive and tedious. So if you want to criticise something for repeating too much, "repetitious" is the stronger and more pointed word.

Repetitious vs. Redundant. "Redundant" means something is not needed because it already exists or has already been said. The focus of "redundant" is on usefulness — this thing serves no purpose. The focus of "repetitious" is on frequency — this thing keeps happening over and over. A sentence can be redundant without being repetitious (said only once, but still unnecessary). And something can be repetitious without every instance being strictly redundant (the repetition is excessive, but each instance isn't entirely without value).

Repetitious vs. Monotonous. "Monotonous" means dull and unchanging, lacking variety. While repetitious things are often monotonous, the two are not the same. Monotony refers to a general sameness or flatness, which doesn't have to come from repetition specifically. A vast empty desert can be monotonous without being repetitious. "Repetitious" specifically points to something repeating — the same content, ideas, or actions appearing again and again.

There is no precise threshold — the judgment depends on context. What's considered repetitious in a sharp, formal business report might be acceptable in a children's educational book, where repetition helps learning. The word always involves a degree of personal or cultural judgment about when repetition has crossed the line. That said, the core question is always: does this repetition serve a purpose, or is it simply padding? If it's the latter, "repetitious" fits.

You can also modify the word to show degree: something can be slightly repetitious, quite repetitious, or extremely repetitious depending on how severe the problem is.

Seeing the word used naturally in context is one of the best ways to truly understand it.

"The professor's lecture was so repetitious that students started losing focus — he restated the same conclusion four times without ever deepening the argument."

"Her novel is beautifully written in places, but the middle section becomes repetitious, cycling through the same emotional beats without pushing the story forward."

"I like my work, but I'll admit the data entry side of it feels repetitious after a while."

"The politician was criticised for giving repetitious speeches — audiences felt they were hearing the same promises reworded at every rally."

"A good editor's job is to cut repetitious passages and make sure every sentence earns its place."

Words that are similar in meaning to "repetitious" include: tedious (long and boring), long-winded (taking far too many words to make a point), redundant (unnecessary because already covered), and pleonastic (a formal word meaning using more words than needed to express an idea). None of these are perfect synonyms — each has its own shade of meaning — but they all share the sense of something that goes on longer or repeats more than it should.

The opposite of repetitious would be words like: concise (saying exactly what needs to be said, no more), varied (involving pleasing change and difference), fresh (new and original), and dynamic (lively, constantly evolving).

"Repetitious" means excessively or tediously repetitive — repeating things more than necessary, to the point of boring or frustrating the audience. It is almost always used as a criticism. The excess is the problem, not the repetition itself. Use this word when something doesn't just repeat, but repeats in a way that adds no value and wears out its welcome.
13639:
To repine means to feel quietly unhappy and discontented with your situation, and to dwell on that unhappiness — often with a sense of self-pity, silent complaint, or helpless resentment.

It is the feeling of sitting with your dissatisfaction rather than doing anything about it. Think of it as a slow, brooding, inward sulking over how things are — or over how things aren't going your way.
Breaking It Down: What It Really Feels Like

Imagine someone who didn't get the life they hoped for. They didn't get the job, or the relationship fell apart, or they feel trapped in circumstances they didn't choose. Instead of accepting it and moving on, or fighting to change it, they sit in it. They quietly brood. They mope. They fret. They silently wish things were different, again and again.

That mental and emotional state — that quiet, persistent, inward dissatisfaction — is exactly what repine captures.

It is not:

  • Screaming rage or loud outburst (that would be too active and explosive)
  • A single passing moment of sadness
  • A strong, purposeful complaint made to someone to fix something

It is:

  • A lingering, low-burning unhappiness
  • A brooding over what you lack or what went wrong
  • A kind of self-indulgent sorrow or fretfulness
  • Often tinged with a feeling that your situation is unfair or unfortunate
The Emotional Texture of the Word

The word carries a slightly negative moral undertone — not harshly judgmental, but gently so. When a writer uses "repine," there's often the implication that the repining is somewhat unproductive or unnecessary. The person repining is seen as someone who won't let go, who keeps picking at the wound of their discontent instead of healing.

This is why you'll often see the word used in phrases like "there is no use in repining" — meaning: stop wallowing, accept reality, and move on.

As a verb, repine is often followed by the prepositions at, over, or about:

  • She repined at her misfortune.
  • He repined over opportunities lost.
  • There is no point repining about what cannot be changed.

It can also be used without a preposition, especially when describing a general state:

  • She sat alone and repined.
  • He spent his days repining.
Examples That Show the Word in Action

1. "After losing the election, he did nothing but repine at his defeat, reliving every mistake in his mind."

Here, the person is brooding over the loss rather than accepting it or trying again.

  1. "She had learned long ago that repining over what she couldn't change only deepened her misery."

Here, repining is the act of dwelling on unchangeable circumstances with quiet bitterness.

  1. "Stop repining and be grateful for what you have."

A direct instruction to someone to stop wallowing in self-pity.

  1. "The old man repined in silence, mourning a life he felt had passed him by."

Here, the silence is key — this is internal, not a vocal complaint made to others.
What Makes "Repine" Different from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention:

  • Complain — you say something out loud to someone. Repining can be completely silent and internal.
  • Grieve — grief is about loss of something specific and dear (like a person). Repining is broader, often about general discontent with one's lot in life.
  • Sulk — sulking often involves a reactive, almost childish refusal to engage. Repining is more melancholy and resigned in character.
  • Fret — fretting has anxious energy to it; you fret about things that might go wrong. Repining is stiller and more backward-looking — you repine over things that have gone wrong or a life you didn't get.
  • Lament — lamenting is more openly expressive, even poetic. Repining is quieter, more private.

If you had to place repine on a spectrum, it sits somewhere between sulk and lament — quieter than lamenting, more melancholy and less reactive than sulking.
Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

Repine is a literary and somewhat archaic word. You will not hear it in everyday casual conversation. You are most likely to encounter it in:

  • Classic novels (19th century literature especially)
  • Poetry
  • Formal or elevated written English
  • Religious or philosophical writing, where the idea of accepting one's fate vs. resisting it is discussed

If you use it in everyday speech, most people may not know it, so it's better reserved for writing or for contexts where a refined vocabulary is appropriate.
To repine is to quietly brood over your dissatisfaction with life or circumstances — dwelling on unhappiness, often helplessly, rather than accepting or acting.
